title: Why PCAP Matters to Blue Team
description: The packet doesn't lie. Why full packet capture is the ultimate source of truth.

slides.title: The Ultimate Source of Truth 📦
slides.content:
# PCAP: Packet Capture

In Chapter 6, we analyzed **logs** (firewall, proxy, DNS). Logs are **summaries** of what happened. But logs can be wrong, incomplete, or missing due to misconfiguration.

**PCAP** is the **raw, unaltered network traffic**. It contains every single byte that crossed the wire.

**Analogy:**
*   **Log:** The security guard's handwritten notes. *"Suspicious person walked by at 2 AM."*
*   **PCAP:** The **high-definition security camera footage**. You can zoom in, rewind, and see exactly what the person was carrying.

**Why SOC Analysts Need PCAP:**
*   Confirm if an attack actually succeeded (Did the TCP handshake complete?)
*   Extract transferred files (Malware samples, stolen data).
*   See **inside** encrypted tunnels (if you have the private key or session key).

slides.title: PCAP vs. NetFlow vs. Logs 📊
slides.content:
# The Pyramid of Network Visibility

| Data Source | Content | Storage Cost | Detail Level |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **NetFlow / IPFIX** | Who talked to whom, how long, bytes count | Very Low | Low (Metadata) |
| **Firewall / Proxy Logs** | Port, URL, Action (Allow/Deny) | Low | Medium |
| **PCAP** | Every byte of every packet | **VERY HIGH** | **Maximum** |

**The Trade-off:** You cannot store full PCAP for all traffic forever. It's too much data. SOCs typically use **rolling buffers** (e.g., 24-72 hours) or capture only on **trigger** (when an alert fires).

**Analyst Note:** If an alert is 3 days old, the PCAP might be **gone**. Act fast.

quizData.question: You need to know the exact contents of a file that was downloaded via HTTP. Which data source provides this?
quizData.explanation: Only PCAP contains the actual file bytes. Proxy logs might have the URL but not the file itself.

slides.title: The Anatomy of a Packet (Simplified)
slides.content: A packet is like a Russian nesting doll.
slides.codeSnippet:
[Ethernet Header] [IP Header] [TCP Header] [HTTP Data / Payload]

- Ethernet: Source/Destination MAC Address.
- IP: Source/Destination IP Address.
- TCP: Source/Destination Port, Flags (SYN, ACK), Sequence Numbers.
- Payload: The actual data (HTML, EXE file, password).

slides.title: The PCAP Goldmine ⛏️
slides.content:
## When Logs Fail, PCAP Saves You

**Scenario:** Firewall log says connection was `ALLOWED`. Proxy log shows `200 OK` for a suspicious URL. But did the malware actually **install**?

**Answer:** Open the PCAP. Look at the **TCP Stream**. If you see a `GET /` request followed by a large binary blob coming back, and then **more connections** to other IPs... you have **proof of compromise**.

**This is why Tier 2/Tier 3 analysts live in Wireshark.**
